clue.text: Is one most surprised to be knocked down by this fighter?

blocks.clueFragment: Is one most surprised to be knocked down
blocks.note: surface reading: someone astonished enough to be bowled over
setter's reading: the idiom says a startled person could be knocked down with a feather, so a boxer named after one fits

explanation.surface: A boxer floors an opponent who can hardly believe it.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'you could have knocked me down with a feather' expresses great surprise; the boxing weight class borrows that light object.
explanation.definitionFit: A featherweight is a boxer in one of the lightest weight divisions, so it is a kind of fighter.

clue.text: When a page got into print soon after Christmas

definitions.text: When a page got into print soon after Christmas

blocks.clueFragment: When a page got into print
blocks.note: surface reading: a sheet of a book going to press
setter's reading: in the carol Good King Wenceslas, the king's page treads in his master's footprints in the snow on 26 December

explanation.surface: A printer recalls the day a page went to press just after Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: The carol Good King Wenceslas opens on Saint Stephen's day, and the page follows his king by stepping in his footprints.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Stephen's day falls on 26 December, the day the carol's page walked in his master's snowy footprints.

clue.text: Moving a common jail

blocks.note: taken as written
stir is a common, slangy word for prison

explanation.surface: Someone is being transferred to an ordinary prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Astir describes people up and about, in motion, so it works as an adjective for moving.

clue.text: A sign that someone found the rider's fall funny

definitions.text: A sign that someone found the rider's fall funny

blocks.note: surface reading: an onlooker showing amusement
setter's reading: the noise suits a mocking laugh at a horseman's tumble, and the word for it contains the animal itself

explanation.surface: A spectator cannot help laughing when a jockey tumbles off.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse-laugh is a loud, coarse guffaw, exactly the noise of someone mocking a mishap.

clue.text: But out of bounds for golfing ing drivers?

blocks.note: surface reading: a part of the golf course where play is not allowed
setter's reading: drivers are motorists, whose fairway is the strip of tarmac that golf balls must avoid; the scan repeats 'ing'

explanation.surface: A golfer is warned that a stretch of ground is out of bounds for their long clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: A driver is both a golf club and a motorist; the motorist's fairway is the golfer's out of bounds.
explanation.definitionFit: The roadway is the part of a street used by vehicles, the drivers' own playing area.

clue.text: "Ice, mast-high, came floating by. As green 11 (Coleridge)

blocks.note: surface reading: a line of polar verse from The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
setter's reading: complete the next line of the poem, which compares the ice to a gemstone

explanation.walkthrough: Coleridge wrote 'And ice, mast-high, came floating by, As green as' a precious stone; the scan shows '11' where the clue had the quotation's continuation.
explanation.definitionFit: The emerald is the classic green gemstone, the comparison Coleridge chose for the drifting icebergs.

clue.text: A challenging sort of 10

blocks.note: surface reading: a difficult or provocative kind of thing
setter's reading: 10 is the hand covering a knight would throw down to issue a challenge

explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to 10 across; a medieval knight threw his gauntlet on the ground as a pledge to fight.
explanation.definitionFit: A gage is a glove or gauntlet flung down as a formal challenge to combat, an archaic word.

clue.text: Was Cadmus's crop so tasty?

blocks.note: surface reading: a harvest raised by a farmer called Cadmus
setter's reading: in Greek myth Cadmus sowed a dragon's teeth, so his crop was literally full of teeth

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a legendary farmer's harvest was delicious.
explanation.walkthrough: Cadmus, founder of Thebes, planted dragon's teeth and armed men sprang up; a field of teeth is 'tooth-some'.
explanation.definitionFit: Toothsome means pleasant to eat, delicious, a slightly old-fashioned synonym for tasty.

clue.text: Rhinelander would never make old bones? On the contrary

definitions.text: Rhinelander would never make old bones? On the contrary

blocks.clueFragment: Rhinelander would never make old bones?
blocks.note: surface reading: a German from the Rhine region is not expected to live long
setter's reading: one early human named after a valley near Düsseldorf is known to us only from very old bones

explanation.surface: A gloomy forecast that a Rhineland native will die young, then overturned.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'make old bones' is to live to old age; the Neander valley lies in the Rhineland, where fossil remains were found in 1856.
explanation.definitionFit: The extinct human species takes its name from the Neander valley in western Germany, where its fossils were first identified.

clue.text: Night and day? So they do

blocks.note: surface reading: something done constantly, around the clock
setter's reading: night and day take turns, each following the other in succession

explanation.definitionFit: To alternate is to take turns repeatedly, as darkness and daylight do in their endless cycle.

clue.text: Hand in this for the Friendly Association

definitions.text: Hand in this for the Friendly Association

blocks.note: surface reading: submit something, as one would a form
setter's reading: the idiom 'hand in' plus the missing word describes close, friendly partnership

explanation.surface: A member is asked to hand in a form to a friendly society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hand in glove' means working in close cooperation, often too close.
explanation.definitionFit: A glove is the garment a hand goes into, completing the idiom for intimate collaboration.

clue.text: Cole's musicians number

blocks.note: surface reading: the band of a performer called Cole
setter's reading: in the nursery rhyme Old King Cole called for his fiddlers, and the rhyme says how many

explanation.surface: A song by a band of musicians named after Cole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' looks like a song; it is a count. Old King Cole 'called for his fiddlers three' in the rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyme gives King Cole's fiddlers as a trio, so the count of his musicians is that figure.

clue.text: Those in the know know its identity

blocks.note: surface reading: insiders who are well informed
setter's reading: the phrase for being well informed is to know this word's own identity, doubled with an 's

explanation.walkthrough: Well-informed people 'know what's what'; read literally, that is knowing the identity of the word itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'what's what' means the true state of affairs, built by asking the interrogative about itself.

clue.text: Avoid attention

blocks.note: first meaning: keep away from deliberately
second meaning: the clipped parade-ground order to stand to attention

explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks you to avoid notice; the second sense is the sergeant-major's bark, short for 'attention!'.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to steer clear of, and the shortened drill command is how soldiers hear the word attention.

clue.text: Make sport-a clue for a gambler

indicators.note: to make sport of something is to play about with it, so the letters that follow are toyed with and rearranged

blocks.note: the letters taken as written, ten in all

explanation.surface: An instruction to turn a crossword clue into a game for a betting man.
explanation.definitionFit: A speculator takes risky positions hoping for profit, a market gambler.

clue.text: It's so wrong sometimes it's pathetic

blocks.note: surface reading: something badly mistaken
setter's reading: the literary term for giving nature human feelings pairs this word with pathetic

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a mistake is so bad it is pitiful.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruskin coined 'pathetic fallacy' for attributing human emotion to weather or landscape.
explanation.definitionFit: A fallacy is a mistaken belief or faulty argument, something that is wrong.

clue.text: Knight at arms in slow motion by the lake

blocks.note: surface reading: an armoured knight on a slow-motion film

blocks.clueFragment: in slow motion by the lake
blocks.note: setter's reading: Keats's La Belle Dame sans Merci finds its knight-at-arms 'alone and palely' doing this, beside a lake with withered sedge

explanation.surface: A knight in armour moves slowly beside a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats: 'O what can ail thee, knight-at-arms, Alone and palely loitering? The sedge has withered from the lake'.
explanation.definitionFit: Loitering is lingering idly, moving about aimlessly and slowly instead of going anywhere.

clue.text: Disapprove of an eccentric old peer

indicators.note: an eccentric is off-centre and odd, so the following words are knocked out of their usual order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone frowns on an odd, aged member of the House of Lords.
explanation.walkthrough: A peer is a member of the British nobility who sits in the House of Lords.
explanation.definitionFit: To deplore something is to condemn it strongly, a forceful way to express disapproval.

clue.text: Annie not so happy getting no man with it?

blocks.note: surface reading: a woman named Annie feeling low
setter's reading: Annie Get Your Gun has the song 'You Can't Get a Man with a Gun', and Annie Oakley was a sharpshooter, quick on the draw

explanation.surface: Annie is unhappy because her gun has not won her a husband.
explanation.walkthrough: Annie Oakley was trigger-happy; drop the 'happy' and the remaining part of the gun is what she fails to get a man with.
explanation.definitionFit: The trigger is the lever of a gun that fires it, the part a trigger-happy shooter squeezes too readily.

clue.text: A lozenge for a flat fish

blocks.note: first meaning: a diamond shape with four equal sides
second meaning: the Latin name for the turbot and its relatives

explanation.surface: Swapping a throat sweet for a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lozenge' suggests a cough sweet, but it is the heraldic diamond shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Geometrically the word names an equilateral parallelogram, and zoologically it names a genus of flatfish including turbot.

clue.text: First person in Germany is inter alias the best off

indicators.note: inter is Latin for among, so the German word is placed among the others that follow

blocks.note: ich is German for I, the first person pronoun
alias is Latin for other things, which are the rest

explanation.surface: Among other things, a leading German is the wealthiest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inter alia' looks like the stock phrase for 'among other things'; split in two, it places ICH inside the others.
explanation.definitionFit: The richest person has the most money, so is the most well off of all.

clue.text: Platform for the beak

blocks.note: first meaning: a raised stand for a speaker or conductor
second meaning: Latin and zoological word for a bird's bill

explanation.surface: A raised stage is set up for the magistrate.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a beak is a magistrate, which makes the platform look like a judge's bench.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a speaker's dais and also, in zoology, a beak-like snout; Roman platforms were decorated with ships' prows.

clue.text: Confused type of rat-catcher

blocks.note: surface reading: a muddled person; to a printer, jumbled metal letters
setter's reading: the same word describes the colourful piper of Hamelin who led the rats away

explanation.walkthrough: Printers call a spilt, jumbled tray of type 'pie', and the Pied Piper of Hamelin piped the rats out of town.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means jumbled when said of printer's type and multicoloured when describing the Hamelin piper.

clue.text: We French have a mind for this

definitions.note: a noun for good sense, not the verb

blocks.note: first meaning: the French pronoun for we
second meaning: common sense, intelligence, from Greek philosophy

explanation.surface: The French claim to have a flair for something.
explanation.definitionFit: In English the Greek-derived word means practical intelligence or common sense, and in French it is the plural pronoun.

clue.text: Snaky bloodsucking old witch

blocks.note: surface reading: an insult hurled at a treacherous, grasping person
setter's reading: a figure of classical myth, half woman and half serpent, who drank children's blood

explanation.surface: A spiteful description of a nasty old woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats wrote a poem about this serpent-woman of Greek legend.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this monster had a woman's upper body and a serpent's tail and preyed on blood.

clue.text: Remit change, for what it's worth

indicators.note: the instruction to change tells you to alter the order of the word next to it

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Sending back the coins, for whatever good that does.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remit change' reads as an instruction to send money back; 'for what it's worth' is a shrugging aside.
explanation.definitionFit: Merit is the quality of deserving praise, a thing's intrinsic value or worth.

clue.text: Father-love goes to the wall

definitions.note: a dado is the lower part of a wall, not the whole wall

blocks.note: an informal word for father
love is zero in tennis, which looks like this letter

explanation.surface: A father's love fails, as a business goes to the wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes to the wall' is the idiom for collapsing; here it only joins the pieces to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A dado is the decorated lower band of an interior wall, often finished with a rail.

clue.text: Laziest possible girl, no saint

indicators.note: possible suggests one arrangement among many that could be made, so the letters are reordered
no says the following abbreviation is to be left out

blocks.note: taken as written
ST is the usual abbreviation for saint

explanation.surface: The idlest girl you could find, and certainly no saint.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the abbreviation from the end of the first word, then rearrange the five letters left.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliza is a girl's name, the short form of Elizabeth, so it is an example of a girl.

clue.text: Artist in Nashville meets potent spirit of the abyss

indicators.note: in places the painter inside the town that follows

blocks.note: Beau Nash was the celebrated master of ceremonies of this Somerset spa town, so it is his ville
RA stands for Royal Academician, an artist
rum is a strong spirit

explanation.surface: A painter in the Tennessee country music city drinks with a demon of the pit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nashville' seems to be the American city; it is Bath, the English spa where Beau Nash ruled society in the 18th century.
explanation.definitionFit: Barathrum, from Greek, means a bottomless pit or chasm, and was also the pit at Athens into which criminals were thrown.

clue.text: Arms go to aid an unusual philanthropist

indicators.note: unusual means out of the ordinary, so the preceding words appear in an unexpected order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written, thirteen in all

explanation.surface: Weapons are sent to help a rare benefactor.
explanation.walkthrough: In Jesus's parable the man from Samaria stops to help a beaten traveller whom others ignore.
explanation.definitionFit: The parable's helper has given his name to anyone who generously helps strangers in need, a kindly benefactor.
